readings.text: “All the Lord’s works are very good, and every command will come to pass at its time. One cannot say, ‘What is this? What is this for?’ For everything will be sought at its time.

31.how: Sirach 39:33 says all the Lord’s works are good and supply every need, echoing the goodness of creation declared in Genesis 1:31.
31.why: It affirms creation’s goodness as a ground for trust.

readings.text: “All the Lord’s works are good, and He will supply every need at its proper hour.

31.how: Genesis 1:23 closes the fifth day with the same evening and morning formula that closes the sixth day in Genesis 1:31.
31.why: It shows the repeated pattern structuring the creation week.

readings.text: And there was evening, and there was morning: a fifth day.

31.how: Genesis 1:8 uses the evening and morning formula for the second day, the same refrain that ends the sixth day in Genesis 1:31.
31.why: It highlights the pattern of the creation days.

readings.text: And God called the firmament Heaven. And God saw that it was good. And there was evening, and there was morning: a second day.

31.how: Genesis 1:5 first uses the evening and morning formula for the first day, which Genesis 1:31 repeats for the sixth day.
31.why: It shows the refrain that frames the whole week.

readings.text: And God called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. And there was evening, and there was morning: one day.

31.how: Genesis 1:19 uses the evening and morning formula for the fourth day, the same pattern that ends the sixth day in Genesis 1:31.
31.why: It shows the repeated structure of the creation days.

readings.text: And there was evening, and there was morning: a fourth day.

31.how: Genesis 1:13 uses the evening and morning formula for the third day, matching the closing of the sixth day in Genesis 1:31.
31.why: It shows the repeated structure of the creation days.

readings.text: And there was evening, and there was morning: a third day.

31.how: Psalm 104:24 (numbered 103 here) praises God for making all things in wisdom, a poetic response to the very good creation of Genesis 1:31.
31.why: It turns the verdict of goodness into praise.

readings.text: How great Thy works have become, Lord! Thou madest all things in wisdom; the earth was filled with Thy possession.

31.how: Psalm 19:1–2 (numbered 18 here) says the heavens and days declare God’s glory, responding to the finished creation that Genesis 1:31 calls very good.
31.why: It shows creation itself bearing witness to its Maker.

readings.text: The heavens recount God’s glory, and the firmament announces the work of His hands.
Day pours forth an utterance to day, and night announces knowledge to night.

31.how: Psalm 104:31 (numbered 103 here) says the Lord rejoices in His works, which matches God’s satisfaction in creation in Genesis 1:31.
31.why: It shows God’s delight in what He made.

readings.text: Let the Lord’s glory be for ever; the Lord will rejoice in His works.

31.how: Lamentations 3:38 asks whether both calamity and good come from the Most High, which loosely engages the theme of God as source of all good raised in Genesis 1:31.
31.why: It presses the question of how a good creation relates to suffering.

readings.text: will not calamities and good come from the mouth of the Most High?

31.how: Job 38:7 describes the stars and angels praising God at creation, loosely linked to the celebration of finished creation implied in Genesis 1:31.
31.why: It adds a picture of creation received with praise.

readings.text: when stars came to be, and all My angels praised Me with a great voice?

31.how: Wisdom 11:24 says God loves all that exists and hates nothing He made, a reflection on the goodness of creation declared in Genesis 1:31.
31.why: It draws out God’s love for everything He made.

readings.text: For Thou lovest all existing things and abhorrest nothing that Thou didst make; for Thou wouldst not have fashioned anything while hating it.

31.how: Sirach 16:26 says God’s works have existed from the beginning and He assigned them their portions, loosely reflecting the ordered creation of Genesis 1:31.
31.why: It presents creation as ordered by God’s judgment.

readings.text: By the Lord’s judgment His works have existed from the beginning; from their making He distinguished their portions.
